strings.calc.fine: The commission math is factual: your revenue × the rate. Rates are indicative and editable: Uber Eats ~25-35%, Deliveroo ~25-30% (indicative ranges, public sources, 2024). “Employer-cost SMIC”: the monthly employer cost of a full-time SMIC (the French minimum wage) — gross SMIC of €1,867.02 as of January 1, 2026 (service-public.gouv.fr), residual employer contributions included (~€1,933). An order of magnitude, not an invoice.
strings.calc.habitues: Your regulars, though, can order direct: commission-free.

strings.combat.aria: Captain.Food pins the commission to the ground
strings.combat.img_alt: Captain Food skewers the “commission” parasite with his golden fork and pins it to the ground
strings.combat.sub: 0% on your dishes, always. Your margin stays in your pocket — not a platform's.
strings.combat.title: The commission? We're taking it down.
strings.esus.p1: Captain.Food starts from a simple conviction: digital tools should serve the public good, not be a tollbooth in the hands of a few tech giants. The problem isn't that they make money — it's that once you depend on them, they can squeeze, and nothing stops them.
strings.esus.p2: So we're building in safeguards that will hold. We're aiming for accreditation as a solidarity-based social utility enterprise (ESUS, a French legal status) — a legal framework that caps profit-taking and locks in the mission — with a cooperative (SCIC) as our destination, where restaurateurs, riders and citizens will have a say. The goal: to be, by design, unable to become what we're fighting.
strings.esus.p3: And so you don't have to take our word for it: we're opening our books in public on Open Collective — every euro received and spent, meant to be visible to everyone. Radical transparency, not a slogan.
strings.esus.p4: Our horizon: for Captain.Food to be a digital commons, not a private asset. The code is open — on GitHub — under the Captain.Food Coopyleft license (a copyleft based on AGPL v3, in the spirit of CoopCycle), whose commercial use is reserved for social and solidarity economy structures — cooperatives and non-profits. Our course: getting it recognized as a digital public good (DPG) — so it's verifiable, and above all replicable: other cities, other cooperatives will be able to take it up. A tool for the common good is meant to be shared — not sold off. Read the manifesto →
strings.esus.rider_body: In the gig economy, the rider is a variable to squeeze — precarious, unprotected. We made the opposite choice: pay our riders better than anyone, here in Tours, with the ambition, in time, to hire them as employees. A fair service starts with people treated right.
strings.esus.rider_link: → How we pay for delivery, in plain words (worked example included)
strings.esus.rider_title: The second fight: riders, paid decently
strings.esus.title: An alternative that can never turn into a tollbooth

strings.faq.a1: For you: 0% commission on your dishes, free signup, no matter what. The service is funded by a pay-what-you-want customer contribution, added to their order in full transparency (€0 is fine, no judgment) — never by you. Card payment fees are the standard banking fees of any online payment, never a surcharge added for the customer. See the full details, worked example included.
strings.faq.a2: Whatever goes through your usual till (on site, at the counter), we don't touch: it's free, full stop — outside our flow. The contribution only applies to orders paid online through Captain.Food.
strings.faq.a3: Delivery will be a future channel, not active yet. The idea: pay the rider properly (we're aiming for at least €7 per ride). You'd only chip in on your delivered orders, up to what your margin allows — you'd set your floor, and we'd never go below it. The customer would pay the difference, transparently. Never a commission on your dishes. See the math in detail, worked example included.
strings.faq.a4: No. Captain.Food comes on top, with no exclusivity. Many restaurants keep both and see Captain.Food as their direct channel — the one they control.
strings.faq.a5: Because it costs you nothing and you give up no exclusivity. You get listed, you recover your customer base from your first direct orders, and you shape the tool while we're starting out. The first ones aboard are the ones who weigh the most.
strings.faq.a6: Every order placed directly on your page belongs to you: you get access to your customers' contact details (with their consent) to build loyalty yourself. Unlike the big platforms, we don't confiscate your customer base.
strings.faq.a7: ESUS stands for “entreprise solidaire d'utilité sociale” — a solidarity-based social utility enterprise, a French accreditation that legally caps profit-taking and requires a social purpose. It's the course we're aiming for — a guarantee, in time, that Captain.Food can never drift into what we denounce.
strings.faq.a8: Two cases. If the customer pays at the till or on site, it's outside our flow: 100% free, we don't touch it. If they pay online via the QR code, a pay-what-you-want contribution can be added, just like for an online order. In every case, under your name, and 0% commission on your dishes.

strings.finance.cue: How we fund ourselves, in plain words →
strings.finance.p1: Fair question — and here's the answer, in plain words.
strings.finance.p2: First, the essential: you, the restaurateur, never pay a commission on your dishes — €0, no matter what. The service isn't funded on your back.
strings.finance.p3: It's funded by a customer contribution at a pay-what-you-want price, added to their order: everyone gives what they want to keep a fair alternative alive. It's a bet — that informed customers would rather support their local businesses than a multinational.
strings.finance.p4: A customer doesn't contribute this time? That's fine: no contribution on that order, and still 0% commission for you. Card payment fees are the standard fees of any online payment — never a percentage on your dishes, never a surcharge added for the customer.
strings.finance.title: “0% commission — so what do you live on?”

strings.problem.card1_body: No way to build loyalty: no usable loyalty scheme, and you end up depending on the platform to get orders at all.
strings.problem.card2_body: To absorb their commission, you inflate your online prices. And you're stuck with forced promotions and algorithm changes you depend on — which hit your ranking.
strings.problem.intro: On the big platforms, every order costs you more than you think.
strings.problem.ratio_punch: On a delivered order, the commission (~30%) weighs up to 10× your net margin (~3%). You do the work, they cash in.
strings.problem.sources: Sources: ~3% average net margin (Observatoire Fiducial, UMIH/GHR/SNARR press release, June 2025); 2024 insolvencies and +80% over two years (Altares 2024, via L'Hôtellerie-Restauration/GHR). An insolvency = safeguard proceedings, receivership or liquidation; about 2 in 3 end in liquidation.
strings.problem.stat_failures: restaurant businesses in insolvency in France in 2024 — that's +80% in two years.
strings.problem.stat_margin: is the average net margin of a restaurant — far less than the ~30% commission taken on every delivered order.
strings.problem.title: They've gone too far!
strings.quote.body: That's what a lot of owners tell themselves. But your prices swell, customers order less — or somewhere else. Those lost orders? You never see them.
strings.quote.kicker: Passing the commission on doesn't cancel it. It just makes your revenue pay for it.
strings.quote.lead: “I don't care, I just pass the commission on in my prices.”
strings.repercuss.aria: Share of the commission passed on to your prices
strings.repercuss.msg100: Your online prices swell noticeably. Customers compare, find you more expensive, and order less — or somewhere else. Your margin looks safe on paper, but the lost sales? You never see them.
strings.repercuss.msg50: You lose on both fronts: your prices still go up (so less volume), and you swallow the other half (so less margin).
strings.repercuss.q: And if you do pass it on? Look:
